\subsection{The Unassociated Source Problem}
\label{sec:5.4}

Having established the theoretical grounds for dark matter subhalo searches in the previous sections, we now turn to the observational reality. The Fermi-LAT catalogs contain a large population of gamma-ray sources with no identified counterpart at other wavelengths, and these unassociated sources have long been recognized as the natural testing ground for DM subhalo searches. We begin by quantifying the unassociated population and the factors that govern association completeness, then survey the prior search efforts that have targeted this population.


\subsubsection{Unassociated Sources in Fermi-LAT Catalogs}
\label{sec:5.4.1}

The Fermi-LAT source catalogs provide the observational foundation for any search for dark matter subhalos among gamma-ray point sources. As discussed in Section~\ref{sec:2.3}, the latest incremental release, the 4FGL-DR4 catalog~\cite{2022ApJS..260...53A, 2023arXiv230712546B}, contains approximately 7,200 sources detected above a significance threshold of $4\sigma$. Of these, 2,428 sources---roughly one third---remain unassociated, meaning that no plausible counterpart has been identified at other wavelengths~\cite{2023arXiv230712546B}. Among the unassociated population, 1,282 sources lie at Galactic latitudes $|b| > 10{{}^\circ}$, where contamination from diffuse Galactic emission is reduced and the search for exotic source populations becomes more tractable.

The distinction between \textit{association} and \textit{identification} carries specific meanings in the Fermi-LAT context. An association is a statistical link between a gamma-ray detection and a candidate counterpart, established primarily through spatial coincidence using Bayesian or likelihood-ratio methods~\cite{2020ApJS..247...33A}. Because associations rely on statistical inference, they carry a known rate of false matches---typically around 2\% for the Bayesian method and up to 10\% for likelihood-ratio associations~\cite{2020ApJS..247...33A}. Firm identification, by contrast, requires direct observational evidence: periodic variability such as pulsations, correlated variability at other wavelengths, or spatial morphology matching an extended source in another band~\cite{2020ApJS..247...33A}. Only 358 sources in the 4FGL catalog satisfy these stricter criteria.

The completeness of the association procedure depends on several observational factors. Brighter sources are far easier to associate: essentially all sources with a test statistic $\mathrm{TS} > 500$ have known counterparts~\cite{2020ApJS..247...33A}. Fainter sources, on the other hand, suffer from larger positional uncertainties that expand the sky region to be searched and dilute the statistical significance of any spatial coincidence. Galactic latitude also plays a strong role. The association fraction drops from approximately 85\% at high latitudes to around 40\% near the Galactic plane~\cite{2020ApJS..247...33A}, both because dense Galactic source fields make confident associations difficult and because X-ray absorption through the disk impedes the detection of background extragalactic counterparts.

The majority of unassociated sources are expected to be ordinary astrophysical objects whose association has failed for instrumental or geometric reasons. Their spectral properties offer direct clues to their nature. At high latitudes, the average photon index of unassociated sources ($\Gamma \approx 2.24$) matches that of blazars of unknown type, suggesting that faint active galactic nuclei (AGNs) dominate this population~\cite{2020ApJS..247...33A}. Closer to the Galactic plane, the spectra soften ($\Gamma \approx 2.42$), consistent with the expected emission of young pulsars~\cite{2020ApJS..247...33A}. Pulsars with unfavorable beaming geometry, which prevents detection of their pulsed emission, and blazars too faint for multi-wavelength follow-up are the most commonly cited explanations for the unassociated population (see also Section~\ref{sec:2.2}).

To date, no unassociated Fermi-LAT source has been confirmed as a dark matter subhalo~\cite{2020ApJS..247...33A, 2022ApJS..260...53A}. This outcome is not unexpected. As discussed in Section~\ref{sec:5.3}, even under optimistic assumptions about the annihilation cross section and J-factor distributions, the most detectable subhalos would produce gamma-ray spectra similar to those of pulsars or soft-spectrum blazars, making individual identification on spectral grounds alone extremely difficult. Nevertheless, the large unassociated population has motivated a sustained effort to search for DM subhalo candidates within it.


\subsubsection{Previous DM Subhalo Searches}
\label{sec:5.4.2}

The search for dark matter subhalos among Fermi-LAT unassociated sources has a decade-long history, progressing through the successive data releases of the telescope. All prior efforts share a common strategy, referred to as \textit{classify-and-count}: a set of DM subhalo candidates is selected from the unassociated population based on their gamma-ray properties, and upper limits on the annihilation cross section $\langle\sigma v\rangle$ are derived under the assumption that the number of true DM subhalos cannot exceed the number of identified candidates~\cite{2010PhRvD..82f3501B, 2012A&A...538A..93Z, 2012ApJ...747..121A, 2019JCAP...07..020C}.

The earliest searches relied on hand-crafted selection criteria applied directly to catalog parameters. Buckley \& Hooper~\cite{2010PhRvD..82f3501B} pioneered this approach by filtering unassociated sources in the 1FGL catalog according to spectral and spatial properties expected from annihilating WIMPs. Subsequent analyses by Zechlin et al.~\cite{2012A&A...538A..93Z} and the Fermi-LAT Collaboration~\cite{2012ApJ...747..121A} refined these criteria and extended the search to the 2FGL catalog. Berlin \& Hooper~\cite{2014PhRvD..89a6014B} and Bertoni et al.~\cite{2015JCAP...12..035B} placed particular emphasis on spatial extension as a potential discriminant, since nearby subhalos may subtend a measurable angular size whose radial profile would follow the DM density distribution rather than the telescope's point-spread function. Schoonenberg et al.~\cite{2016JCAP...05..028S} and Hooper \& Witte~\cite{2017JCAP...04..018H} applied updated theoretical predictions for DM gamma-ray emission to the 3FGL catalog. Calore et al.~\cite{2017PhRvD..96f3009C} provided realistic detectability estimates, while Coronado-Bl\'azquez et al.~\cite{2019JCAP...07..020C} performed a comprehensive spectral and spatial analysis identifying 16 candidate sources, and in a companion paper~\cite{2019JCAP...11..045C} derived the best achievable sensitivity of the 3FGL catalog under the assumption that zero unassociated sources are subhalos. A common thread across these analyses is that none of the identified candidates could be unambiguously distinguished from standard astrophysical sources: the gamma-ray spectrum of a DM subhalo can be equally well fit by a faint AGN or pulsar template, and the extension searches returned null results for all candidates.

More recently, machine learning classifiers have been applied to automate and extend the candidate selection. Mirabal et al.~\cite{2016ApJ...825...69M} used supervised classification on the 3FGL catalog to evaluate pulsar and DM subhalo interpretations of the high-latitude unassociated population. Germ\'an et al.~\cite{2023MNRAS.520.1348G} constructed a generative model for Fermi-LAT sources incorporating systematic features, while Butter et al.~\cite{2023JCAP...07..033B} applied Bayesian neural networks to the 4FGL catalog. In their most conservative classification scenario, Butter et al.\ identified 281 DM subhalo candidates. The resulting upper limits on $\langle\sigma v\rangle$ are correspondingly weak: the analysis assumes that the true number of subhalos cannot exceed this candidate count, and a different probability threshold would yield a different number and therefore different physical bounds.

A general weakness of the classify-and-count approach, whether carried out with hand-crafted cuts or ML classifiers, is that the final physical constraints depend on choices that lack a rigorous statistical foundation. Three problems are particularly severe. First, in ML-based analyses the number of DM candidates depends on an ad hoc probability threshold: setting $p_{\mathrm{DM}} > 0.5$ versus $p_{\mathrm{DM}} > 0.9$ can change the candidate count by an order of magnitude, with no statistical principle to prefer one threshold over another. Second, the classification probabilities themselves are calibrated on balanced training sets that use an artificial 50/50 split of astrophysical and DM-like sources. Since the true prevalence of DM subhalos is unknown and likely very small, this balanced training inflates the predicted DM probabilities relative to reality. Correcting this bias requires a realistic testing dataset of confirmed DM subhalos---which does not exist. Third, all classify-and-count methods implicitly assume that the feature distribution of unassociated sources matches that of the associated training set, an assumption violated by the systematic differences documented in Section~\ref{sec:5.4.1} and analyzed formally in Section~\ref{sec:3.4}. These failures of classical classification motivate the shift toward quantification learning developed in the next section.
